label: Railway standard gauge, 1435 mm
source_note: Standard gauge is specified as 1435 mm (4 ft 8.5 in).
notes: EXACT specification, not a typical value — the strongest metric anchor available in a railway scene. Measured between the INNER faces of the two railheads, NOT rail centre to rail centre (~1.5 m); marking the wrong edges is a ~4% error that looks entirely reasonable. Mark it near the camera: a wider pixel span measures better.

label: Railway metre gauge, 1000 mm
source_note: Metre gauge is specified as 1000 mm.
notes: A SEPARATE id rather than a tolerance on standard gauge — 1.000 and 1.435 must never silently substitute for each other, since picking the wrong one is a silent 44% scale error. Confirm the network before using this.

label: Railway Cape gauge, 1067 mm
source_note: Cape gauge is specified as 1067 mm (3 ft 6 in).
notes: Common in southern Africa, Japan, Indonesia, Queensland and New Zealand. Separate id for the same reason as metre gauge — never substitute.

label: Railway sleeper spacing, ~0.6 m
source_note: Typical mainline sleeper spacing, ~600 mm centre to centre.
notes: TYPICAL, not specified — varies by network, line speed and sleeper type (roughly 0.60-0.75 m). Weaker than gauge on two counts: the number is approximate, and a single pitch is a short pixel span. Its value is that it repeats down the track, so several marked pitches aggregate. Prefer gauge whenever both are visible.

label: UK station platform height, 915 mm
source_note: UK standard platform height is 915 mm above rail level.
notes: REGIONAL, unlike gauge — platform heights differ widely by country (roughly 0.55-1.25 m), so this is only usable when the location is known to be UK. Vertical: measured from rail level to platform surface, so its base is the RAILHEAD, not the ballast.
